title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt
subtitle: A payment intermediary for clean power in developing countries
message: Investors price the risk that a state distribution company will not pay. A payment intermediary buys power under one standard contract, pays generators in full and on time, and recovers arrears behind a guarantee waterfall agreed in advance.

problem.title: The buyer, not the plant, sets the price

stats.label: cost of the same solar plant at a 12% cost of capital (6.5 c/kWh) against 4% (3.6 c/kWh)
of solar cost was financing in developing economies in 2021; 25–30% in advanced economies
tariff premium for offtaker payment risk, worth 1.4 points on the WACC (stylized)

problem.text: The buyer is usually a loss-making state distribution company: only two of 39 Sub-Saharan African power sectors were financially viable. Investors price how long its arrears last and how much is recovered into every project that sells to it.

mechanism.title: Guarantee the contract, not the debt
mechanism.caption: Stylized 100 MW solar plant: saving to the buyer and the guarantor's expected cost, $ million a year.
points: Coverage: removes payment risk for equity as well as debt, and for every project selling to the same buyer.
Cost: the guarantor pays arrears and recovers them. $5.3 saved per dollar of expected cost; a debt guarantee saves $0.8.
Waterfall, agreed in advance: offtaker, its state owner, a national transfer intercept, a multilateral agency, a donor account.

action.title: Build the intermediary, then fix the buyers
results: India's SECI (AAA) sells about 60 GW at Rs 2.93/kWh on a 7-paise margin.
But weak distributors needed a Rs 90,000 crore liquidity scheme (2020) and rescheduling of Rs 1.4 lakh crore of arrears (2022).
The state's exposure shrinks but stays: national calls about 2% of contract payments in a 2 GW regional facility.
todo: Create or join a facility with one standard PPA and a waterfall signed before the first tender.
